content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published the second edition of its guidelines for the screening and treatment of cervical pre-cancer lesions to prevent cervical cancer. This document is available in both electronic and print formats, with respective ISBNs 978-92-4-003082-4 and 978-92-4-003083-1. Cervical cancer remains a leading cause of mortality among women worldwide. In 2020, approximately 604,000 women were diagnosed with cervical cancer, and 342,000 died from the disease. It is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in 23 countries and the leading cause of cancer-related deaths in 36 countries, primarily in sub-Saharan Africa, Melanesia, South America, and Southeast Asia. In May 2018, WHO Director-General Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus issued a call to action to eliminate cervical cancer. This was followed in November 2020 by the launch of a global strategy to accelerate its elimination, with targets for 2030 including 90% HPV vaccination coverage among eligible girls, 70% screening coverage with a high-performance test, and 90% appropriate management of women with positive screening results or cervical lesions. To achieve these targets, WHO convened a panel of experts to identify key areas for improving access to screening and treatment. One focus area was updating existing WHO recommendations for cervical cancer prevention and simplifying clinical algorithms. The updated guidelines were developed through a systematic process that included reviewing current recommendations, identifying areas for updates or new development, and conducting systematic reviews and modeling outcomes where primary research was unavailable. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology was applied to assess evidence certainty and develop recommendations. The guidelines recommend using HPV DNA detection as the primary screening test instead of visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) or cytology for both the general population of women and women living with HIV. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-certainty evidence. For women living with HIV, WHO suggests starting regular cervical cancer screening at age 25, as evidence indicates a low likelihood of cervical cancer in this group below that age. Screening can be stopped after age 50 if two consecutive negative results are obtained within the recommended screening intervals. Priority should be given to screening women aged 30–49 years in the general population. The guidelines also outline two approaches to screening and treatment: the screen-and-treat approach, where treatment is based on a positive primary screening test, and the screen, triage, and treat approach, where treatment decisions are based on a positive primary test followed by a positive triage test. For triage, options such as partial genotyping, colposcopy, VIA, or cytology may be used, depending on feasibility, training, and resources in different settings. WHO recommends transitioning to HPV DNA testing as the primary screening method during routine screening intervals, even in programs currently using cytology or VIA. For women with histologically confirmed adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS), large-loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ) or cold knife conization (CKC) is suggested, with LLETZ preferred for women of reproductive age in settings with adequate expertise. The guidelines include 23 recommendations and 7 good practice statements, with some recommendations being identical for both the general population and women living with HIV, while others are specific to each group. WHO emphasizes the importance of treating women as soon as possible within six months of a positive screening result to reduce the risk of loss to follow-up, except in cases of pregnancy, where treatment should be deferred until after delivery. These guidelines were developed with contributions from the WHO Guideline Development Group (GDG), the External Review Group (ERG), and other experts. The process was supported by systematic reviews, mathematical modeling, and consultations with stakeholders. Funding for the guideline development was provided by the UNDP-UNFPA-UNICEF-WHO-World Bank Special Programme of Research, Development, and Research Training in Human Reproduction (HRP), with additional support from PEPFAR, USAID, and Unitaid.
